This method increases energy efficiency 1 by allowing higher coolant temperatures and lower airflow, reducing energy use. However, its flexibility is limited by the need for tailored enclosures and pipework specific to each data center’s layout. In addition, DTC systems still require air cooling infrastructure to cool other server components. DTC also restricts easy access to servers, a problem partially solved by quick-disconnect connectors that, however, raise leak risks. In addition, these hybrid air-liquid systems incur inherent design and fabrication costs for cold plates, redundant pumps, plumbing, quick disconnects, controls, and heat exchangers, plus their performance is often constrained by thermal interfaces [9]. The initial research on immersion cooling that specifically employed liquid dielectrics for computer cooling was carried out in 1966 by Oktay Sevgin at IBM [10]. The primary distinctions in immersion cooling technology hinge on whether single- or two-phase processes are used within a contained chassis or an open bath setup [11]. In other words, immersion cooling can be categorized as single-phase immersion cooling (1PIC) and 2PIC. 1PIC involves circulating a dielectric fluid over IT components and employing heat exchangers. The fluid in this method is heated and cooled while remaining in its liquid state throughout the entire cycle. 2PIC relies on a pool boiling process to dissipate heat from IT equipment, with the vapor being condensed back to liquid via a condenser [12]. 2PIC has advantages over 1PIC in terms of heat dissipation capacity, cooling efficiency, and the simplicity of the design. Efficiency-wise, 2PIC achieves higher efficiency than 1PIC and that results in significant energy savings [13], [14]. 2PIC also offers cost savings by eliminating the need for a high-capacity pump to circulate dielectric fluid [15]. In other words, 2PIC uses latent heat effectively, thus leading to a higher heat dissipation capacity and efficiency. Note that 2PIC uses a dielectric liquid that requires proper design and maintenance to minimize fluid losses and to remove infiltrating air and humidity from the system through a proper degassing system [16], [7]. Dielectric fluids are critical components in immersion cooling systems, acting as efficient mediums for heat dissipation from electronic components. These specialized fluids feature high dielectric strength and a low dielectric constant and dissipation factor that enables them to serve as an insulating medium for electrically charged components while effectively removing heat. Their nonconductive nature also reduces the risk of electrical shorts and corrosion, making them a dependable option for improving cooling performance across various electronic applications [4]. Some of the widely used two-phase dielectric fluids include FC-72, FC-3284, Novec-7000, Novec-7100, and Novec-649. However, there are concerns associated with many of these fluids. For instance, the chemical stability of Novec-649 in the presence of contaminants, such as water, can necessitate stringent engineering controls to ensure its effective and reliable use in cooling systems [17].
